title: XLA, Hyper-IgM and Reading Vaccine Titres
summary: Learn where X-linked agammaglobulinaemia and the hyper-IgM (class-switch) syndromes break antibody production, how their immunoglobulin patterns and lymphoid tissue differ, and the rules for interpreting vaccine responses on IVIG and in young children.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 52 Hits 4 (XLA), 5 (hyper-IgM part) and 13 (vaccine-titre rules) and Traps 5 and 6. Checked against El-Sayed 2019, Cardenas-Morales 2022, Jhamnani 2018, Perez 2017, Hansen 2021, ICON 2016 (Bonilla; read via a page-fetch tool) and the CDC/ACIP Altered Immunocompetence page (read via a page-fetch tool). Discrepancies: Hit 4’s “NEVER give live vaccines” is broader than the CDC table, which lists specific contraindicated live vaccines for severe antibody deficiency and does not list varicella or rotavirus (register rv-xla-live-vaccine-list; US guidance only, Philippine rules not covered); Hit 13’s fixed 5–6-month IVIG hold was not found in the sources read: the US practice parameter (as summarised by Perez 2017) stops IgG for 4–6 months before re-evaluating stable specific-antibody-deficiency patients, and Hansen 2021 excluded measurements within 6 months of IgG (register rv-ivig-hold-interval). Not taught: hyper-IgE (STAT3/DOCK8) and the IgE figures in Hit 5, the age at which isohemagglutinins form (Hit 13), and UNG beyond its role in switching.

objectives: Locate the XLA and hyper-IgM defects on the B-cell development and class-switch pathway.
Distinguish XLA from hyper-IgM syndromes by B-cell count, immunoglobulin pattern, lymphoid tissue and infections.
Apply the rules for interpreting vaccine responses on immunoglobulin therapy and in children under 2 years, and name live vaccines contraindicated in severe antibody deficiency.

scenes.title: Three boys, three antibody puzzles
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three boys referred for recurrent infections — (1) 18 months, recurrent pneumonia and otitis, tonsils barely visible, IgG, IgA and IgM all very low, CD19+ B cells under 1%; (2) 2 years, Pneumocystis pneumonia, IgM high, IgG and IgA low, normal B-cell count; (3) 14 months, on intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), pneumococcal titres “look protective”. Question token: “Which defect, and which result can you trust?”

cues.text: Three boys with recurrent infections. The first has almost no tonsils, every immunoglobulin class is very low, and B cells are under one percent.
The second has Pneumocystis pneumonia, a high IgM, low IgG and IgA, and a normal B-cell count. The third is on IVIG, and his pneumococcal titres look protective.
Which defect does each boy have, and which result can you actually trust?

lines: Tiny tonsils · all Ig very low

scenes.title: From B cell to switched antibody
scenes.altText: Schematic two-stage pathway. Stage 1, bone marrow: pro-B cell → pre-B cell → mature B cell; Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) is needed to get past the pro-B to pre-B step. Stage 2, germinal centre of a lymph node: CD40 ligand (CD40L) on an activated CD4+ T cell binds CD40 on the B cell; CD40 signalling upregulates activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID); AID and uracil N-glycosylase (UNG) start DNA breaks in the heavy-chain switch regions, which are repaired and rejoined, so the B cell swaps IgM for IgG, IgA or IgE while keeping the same antigen specificity.

cues.text: Antibody production has two stages. First, in the bone marrow, B cells mature from pro-B to pre-B to mature B cells. Bruton tyrosine kinase, BTK, is needed to get past the pro-B to pre-B step.
Mature B cells start out making IgM. Switching to IgG, IgA or IgE happens later, mostly in germinal centres of lymph nodes, and mostly with T-cell help.
The helper signal is CD40 ligand on an activated CD4 T cell binding CD40 on the B cell. That switches on the enzyme AID.
AID and UNG start DNA breaks in the heavy-chain switch regions, which are then repaired and rejoined. The cell swaps IgM for IgG, IgA or IgE but keeps the same antigen specificity.

props.label: Mature B cell starts with IgM

scenes.title: Two places the line can break
scenes.altText: Left card, X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (XLA): BTK gene on the X chromosome; block at pro-B → pre-B; fewer than 2% CD19+ B cells in blood; all immunoglobulin classes severely low; B-lineage cells missing from tissues, so lymph nodes and tonsils are small; about 85% of congenital agammaglobulinaemia. Right card, hyper-IgM (class-switch recombination) syndromes: normal or high IgM with low IgG, IgA and IgE. CD40L deficiency: X-linked, B cells present but switched memory B cells very low, lymph nodes lack germinal centres, a combined immunodeficiency with opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium). AID deficiency: mostly autosomal recessive, the most commonly identified recessive form, mainly an antibody defect, with lymphoid hyperplasia.

cues.text: Break the first stage and you get X-linked agammaglobulinaemia. The BTK gene sits on the X chromosome. B-cell development stalls at the pro-B to pre-B step.
Fewer than two percent of blood lymphocytes are CD19 positive B cells, every immunoglobulin class is very low, and with no B-lineage cells the tonsils and lymph nodes stay small.

Break the second stage and you get a hyper-IgM syndrome: IgM normal or high, but IgG, IgA and IgE low. In X-linked CD40 ligand deficiency the B cells are there, but T-cell help fails too, so opportunists like Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium appear.
In AID deficiency, usually autosomal recessive, mainly antibody production is hit, and lymph nodes can actually enlarge.

props.title: Hyper-IgM (switch fails)
lines: IgM normal/high · IgG, IgA, IgE low

props.label: AID (mostly AR): antibody defect · big nodes

scenes.title: Rules for reading vaccine responses
scenes.altText: Rule cards. (1) IgG replacement products carry donor antibodies, including antibodies to common live viral vaccines, so titres measured on therapy cannot be taken as the patient’s own (ICON 2016); the wait off therapy varies by source: the AAAAI/ACAAI/JCAAI practice parameter (as summarised by Perez 2017) lets stable specific-antibody-deficiency patients stop IgG for 4–6 months and then re-evaluates, and a Danish audit (Hansen 2021) excluded measurements within 6 months of IgG. (2) Pure polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) gives a T-cell-independent response and is not reliably immunogenic before age 2, so specific antibody deficiency is not diagnosed before age 2; post-vaccination titres are drawn about 4 weeks later. (3) Live vaccines in severe antibody deficiency (CDC/ACIP table): MMR, MMRV, oral polio, live influenza, BCG, oral typhoid, yellow fever and smallpox are contraindicated; IVIG also blunts the response to measles vaccine. Hook answers: (1) XLA; (2) CD40L-type hyper-IgM; (3) titres reflect IVIG — cannot be trusted.

cues.text: Immunoglobulin products contain donor antibodies, so titres drawn on IVIG cannot be taken as the patient’s own. Sources differ on the wait: a US practice parameter re-evaluates stable patients after four to six months off IgG.

Pure polysaccharide vaccine needs no T-cell help, and children under two do not respond reliably. So specific antibody deficiency is not diagnosed before age two. Post-vaccine titres are drawn about four weeks later.

In severe antibody deficiencies such as XLA, US guidance lists measles-mumps-rubella, oral polio, live influenza, BCG, oral typhoid and yellow fever as contraindicated. IVIG also blunts the response to measles vaccine.
Back to the hook. Boy one has XLA. Boy two fits CD40 ligand-type hyper-IgM. Boy three’s titres belong to his IVIG, so they cannot be trusted.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Hyper-IgM means too much of every immunoglobulin” (✓ only IgM is normal or high; IgG, IgA and IgE are low — a class-switch failure); “Small or absent tonsils point to a T-cell defect” (✓ that is XLA: no B-lineage cells, so lymphoid tissue stays small); “Good titres on IVIG mean immunity is intact” (✓ the antibodies are the donor’s; re-test off therapy).

cues.text: Trap one: hyper-IgM means too much of every immunoglobulin. No: only IgM is normal or high. IgG, IgA and IgE are low, because switching fails.
Trap two: small or absent tonsils point to a T-cell defect. No: that is XLA. Without B-lineage cells, the lymphoid tissue stays small.
Trap three: good titres on IVIG prove immunity is intact. No: those antibodies came from donors. Re-test off therapy.

props.title: ✗ “Hyper-IgM = too much of every Ig.”
lines: ✓ Only IgM up · IgG, IgA, IgE low

scenes.title: No factory, or a stuck switch
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “XLA: the B-cell FACTORY never opens — no B cells, no antibody of any class, no tonsils. Hyper-IgM: the factory runs but the SWITCH is stuck on M. IVIG: BORROWED money — you cannot judge someone’s income from a loan.” Tokens: no factory = XLA · stuck switch = hyper-IgM · borrowed money = IVIG titres. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: in XLA the B-cell factory never opens, so there are no B cells, no antibody of any class and almost no tonsils. In hyper-IgM the factory runs, but the switch is stuck on M. And titres on IVIG are borrowed money.

Where it breaks: some XLA is leaky, with a little immunoglobulin; CD40 ligand deficiency also cripples T-cell help, so it is a combined defect; and in AID deficiency lymph nodes can enlarge rather than shrink.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “No B cells + all Ig low + tiny tonsils = XLA · IgM up, IgG/IgA/IgE down = class-switch failure”, “Titres on IVIG are donor antibody · polysaccharide unreliable under 2 · avoid listed live vaccines”.

cues.text: Absent B cells with every immunoglobulin low and tiny tonsils means X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, normal or high IgM with low switched classes means a class-switch defect, and vaccine titres measured on immunoglobulin therapy cannot be taken as the patient’s own.

props.label: No B cells + all Ig low = XLA · IgM up, rest down = switch defect
IVIG titres = donor antibody · polysaccharide unreliable < 2 y

explanation.what: Plain language: making antibodies needs B cells to grow up in the bone marrow, then get a signal from T cells to switch from the first antibody (IgM) to the others. XLA breaks the first step, so there are no B cells and no antibodies; hyper-IgM breaks the switch, so IgM is made but IgG, IgA and IgE are not. Scientific terms: Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK), pro-B and pre-B cells, CD19, X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (XLA), class-switch recombination (CSR), CD40 ligand (CD40L), CD40, activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), uracil N-glycosylase (UNG), germinal centre, immunoglobulin replacement (IVIG/SCIG), pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23), T-cell-independent response.
explanation.why: BTK is needed for B-cell development, so in XLA B-lineage cells are almost absent, all immunoglobulin classes are very low and lymphoid tissue is small. CD40L–CD40 signalling switches on AID, which performs class switching; when this pathway fails, IgM persists but switched isotypes are low. CD40L also provides T-cell help, so its deficiency is a combined immunodeficiency with opportunistic infections.
explanation.measure: XLA: CD19+ B cells < 2% with hypogammaglobulinaemia, BTK mutation or defective BTK protein expression, or an affected maternal male relative (Winkelstein criteria as cited by Cardenas-Morales 2022). Hyper-IgM: normal or elevated IgM, low IgG, IgA and IgE; CD40L expression and CD40-binding studies, AID genetics. Vaccine responses: titres about 4 weeks after vaccination; not the patient’s own on IgG therapy (ICON 2016: interpretation must be adjusted and this is not standard practice); the wait off therapy varies by source (4–6 months in the US practice parameter for specific antibody deficiency; 6 months in Hansen 2021); polysaccharide responses not reliable before age 2.
explanation.differs: XLA (no B cells, all Ig low, small tonsils) vs CD40L hyper-IgM (B cells present, IgM normal/high, no germinal centres, opportunistic infections) vs AID deficiency (B cells present, IgM high, lymphoid hyperplasia, mainly bacterial sinopulmonary infections).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the defect from an immunoglobulin pattern and B-cell count, recognise that small tonsils point to XLA, reject vaccine titres drawn on IVIG, and identify live vaccines to withhold in a boy with XLA.

comparisons.title: XLA vs hyper-IgM (CD40L)
comparisons.distinguisher: B cells absent vs present but unable to class-switch.

comparisons.title: CD40L vs AID deficiency
comparisons.distinguisher: T-cell help lost (opportunists) vs B-cell switching enzyme lost (enlarged lymphoid tissue).

mnemonic.text: XLA: the B-cell FACTORY never opens — no B cells, no antibody of any class, no tonsils. Hyper-IgM: the factory runs but the SWITCH is stuck on M. IVIG titres are BORROWED money.
mnemonic.explanation: Separates absent B-cell production, failed class switching and passively acquired antibody.
mnemonic.limitation: Some XLA is leaky with residual immunoglobulin; CD40L deficiency is a combined T- and B-cell defect; AID deficiency can enlarge lymphoid tissue rather than shrink it.

analogyLimitations: Live-vaccine list follows US CDC/ACIP guidance; local schedules and rules differ.
takeaway: Absent B cells with every immunoglobulin low and tiny tonsils means X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, normal or high IgM with low switched classes means a class-switch defect, and vaccine titres measured on immunoglobulin therapy cannot be taken as the patient’s own.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy has Pneumocystis pneumonia. IgM is elevated, IgG and IgA are low, and the CD19+ B-cell count is normal. Which defect best fits?

options.rationale: Correct. Failed CD40L–CD40 signalling blocks class switching (high IgM, low IgG/IgA) and T-cell help, explaining the opportunistic infection with B cells present.
Incorrect. XLA has fewer than 2% B cells and all immunoglobulin classes low, including IgM.
Incorrect. AID deficiency also gives high IgM, but it is mainly an antibody defect; opportunistic infections are not typical.
Incorrect. UNG deficiency is a very rarely reported autosomal recessive class-switch defect affecting mainly antibody production; opportunistic infections are rarely seen.

questions.stem: Which finding best supports X-linked agammaglobulinaemia rather than a T-cell defect in an 18-month-old boy with recurrent pneumonia?

options.text: Very small tonsils with CD19+ B cells below 2% and all immunoglobulin classes low
options.rationale: Correct. Absent B-lineage cells leave tonsils and lymph nodes small and all classes low.

options.text: Normal B cells with high IgM
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is a class-switch (hyper-IgM) pattern.

options.text: B cells present, but class-switched memory B cells absent
options.rationale: Incorrect. This fits a class-switch defect such as CD40L deficiency, in which mature B cells are present.

options.text: Normal IgG, IgA and IgM levels
options.rationale: Incorrect. XLA causes severely decreased production of all classes.

questions.stem: A child receiving monthly IVIG has protective pneumococcal titres. How should the laboratory interpret them?

options.text: They may reflect donor antibody; specific antibody function must be assessed off therapy
options.rationale: Correct. IgG products contain donor antibodies, so titres on therapy cannot be taken as the child’s own; assessment needs a period off therapy (4–6 months in the US practice parameter for specific antibody deficiency).

options.text: They prove the child’s antibody production is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. The measured antibody may not be the child’s own.

options.text: They show IVIG can now be stopped permanently
options.rationale: Incorrect. Titres on therapy cannot show the child’s own antibody function.

options.text: Repeat the titres one week after the next infusion
options.rationale: Incorrect. Titres drawn on therapy still include donor antibody; the patient’s own response needs assessment off therapy.

references.citation: Jhamnani RD, Nunes-Santos CJ, Bergerson J, Rosenzweig SD. Class-Switch Recombination (CSR)/Hyper-IgM (HIGM) Syndromes and Phosphoinositide 3-Kinase (PI3K) Defects. Front Immunol. 2018;9:2172. doi:10.3389/fimmu.2018.02172

references.citation: Perez E, Bonilla FA, Orange JS, Ballow M. Specific Antibody Deficiency: Controversies in Diagnosis and Management. Front Immunol. 2017;8:586. doi:10.3389/fimmu.2017.00586

Perez does not itself state that IgG products contain vaccine antibodies.

references.citation: Bonilla FA, Barlan I, Chapel H, et al. International Consensus Document (ICON): Common Variable Immunodeficiency Disorders. J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract. 2016;4(1):38-59. doi:10.1016/j.jaip.2015.07.025
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool (first part of the page only). Therapeutic IgG contains neutralising antibodies to common live viral vaccines; using standard vaccines to assess responsiveness on IgG therapy is not standard practice; only inactivated or subunit vaccines if CVID is suspected.

references.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Altered Immunocompetence. General Best Practice Guidelines for Immunization (ACIP). Page dated June 26, 2024.
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool. Table 8-1, severe antibody deficiencies (XLA, CVID): contraindicated OPV, smallpox, LAIV, BCG, Ty21a, yellow fever, MMR, MMRV, dengue vaccine; varicella and rotavirus not listed; IGIV interferes with response to measles and possibly varicella vaccine. Narrative: patients with quantitative B-cell deficiencies on immunoglobulin therapy should not receive live or non-live vaccines during that therapy; persons with impaired humoral immunity may receive varicella vaccine. US guidance only.

claims.text: B-cell development (BTK at pro-B to pre-B) and class-switch mechanism (CD40L–CD40, AID, UNG).
XLA: BTK, X-linked, < 2% CD19+ B cells, all classes low, small tonsils/nodes, ~85% of agammaglobulinaemia.
Hyper-IgM pattern; CD40L (X-linked, combined, opportunists, no germinal centres) vs AID (AR, lymphoid hyperplasia).

Titres on IgG therapy may reflect product antibody; assess off therapy (4–6 months in the US practice parameter for SAD; 6 months in Hansen 2021); polysaccharide unreliable under 2; titres ~4 weeks after vaccination.
Live vaccines contraindicated in severe antibody deficiency (US list); IVIG blunts measles vaccine response.
claims.note: US CDC/ACIP guidance; Philippine rules not covered.

claims.text: Hyper-IgE (STAT3, DOCK8) and IgE thresholds; age at which isohemagglutinins form.
claims.note: Not taught as facts in this lesson.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 52 Hit 4 says XLA patients must “NEVER” receive live vaccines. The CDC/ACIP Altered Immunocompetence table lists specific contraindicated live vaccines for severe antibody deficiencies (OPV, smallpox, LAIV, BCG, Ty21a, yellow fever, MMR, MMRV, dengue) and does not list varicella or rotavirus (its narrative says persons with impaired humoral immunity may receive varicella vaccine); it also notes IVIG interferes with measles (and possibly varicella) vaccine responses, and that patients with quantitative B-cell deficiencies on immunoglobulin therapy should not receive live or non-live vaccines during that therapy, so in practice the reviewer’s advice largely holds for a treated XLA patient. This is US guidance; Philippine rules are not covered (register flag rv-xla-live-vaccine-list).

Ch. 52 Hit 13 gives a fixed 5–6-month IVIG hold before evaluating vaccine responses. No source read states that interval: the US practice parameter, as summarised by Perez 2017, lets stable specific-antibody-deficiency patients stop IgG for 4–6 months and then re-evaluates; Hansen 2021 excluded measurements within 6 months of IgG therapy. The lesson teaches that the wait varies by source (register flag rv-ivig-hold-interval).
